storm.summary_layperson: A Severe Thunderstorm Watch remains posted for the region until 8 PM, but the strongest storms (up to 56 dBZ) are already 20+ miles north of the cove and pulling away — the immediate threat to Greenwich is low and easing through the evening.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's cooling marine layer isn't a factor tonight since the retreating storms are exiting north instead of crossing the water toward the cove; that gap (9°F now) would fade below the roughly 5°F protective threshold by about 6:46 PM anyway.
storm.detail_html:
Severe thunderstorms have been rolling through the region all afternoon. NWS Upton issued Severe Thunderstorm Watch #544 for the Lower Hudson Valley, northeast New Jersey, and much of southern Connecticut, in effect until 8 PM, with the area forecast discussion citing mid-level instability (MLCAPE) over 2,000 J/kg and wind shear around 20 kt supporting strong to severe storms into early evening.

Radar out of KOKX shows a cluster of cells 20–29 miles north to north-northwest of the cove, several topping 54–56 dBZ — but they're tracking away from the cove at roughly 59 kt toward the north-northeast. That's the system exiting the area, not approaching it, and the arrival-prediction engine confirms no cell is currently closing on Greenwich Cove.

Normally the Sound's cooler water (75°F versus 84°F air, a 9°F gap) works to weaken a storm that has to cross it before reaching shore. That mechanism doesn't apply tonight because these cells are moving out on an inland track that bypasses the Sound entirely — the protective effect is simply not in play for this batch. For the record, that 9°F gap is fading fast anyway as the evening cools: it drops below the roughly 5°F threshold that keeps the marine layer meaningfully protective by about 6:46 PM, so even a redeveloping cell later tonight wouldn't get much benefit from it.

The watch technically covers the wider region until 8 PM, so towns closer to the retreating cells — northern Westchester, the Hudson Valley — could still see leftover activity. The cove itself sits outside the current cells' path.

What would change the call: CAPE stays elevated (roughly 1,000–2,400 J/kg per HRRR) through the evening, and the AFD flags a continued threat of isolated to scattered storms into early evening, with another round possible Monday. Any new cell development along a sea-breeze convergence line to the west or southwest later tonight would be worth watching — the instability hasn't gone away, only this particular batch of cells has moved on.

wind.tactics_blurb: Sea breeze reinforced by the background southwesterly wind — expect WSW 6-7 kt easing gradually to SW 5 kt by 10 PM rather than a hard sunset collapse. Pressure is fairly even across the cove with a slight edge toward the east shore/mouth; don't overcommit to one side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The air–water temperature gap (about 9°F, inland air near 84°F versus Sound water 75°F) clears the roughly 5°F threshold needed to build a sea breeze, and today's background gradient wind (about 9.7 kt, from the well-sited airport network) is onshore from the southwest rather than opposing it. That combination — thermal driver present, gradient reinforcing instead of fighting — makes this a sea breeze reinforced by the background wind, not a pure thermal day and not a gradient-only day.

HRRR's model wind is running about 15° behind the real sea breeze direction: the model has it at SW 233° while Riverside YC and the western-Sound station cluster are already reading WSW 248°. That's a known model lag during sea-breeze maturation. We've used the corrected WSW direction for the front half of the window and let HRRR's own natural backing trend carry the later hours as the thermal fades into pure gradient flow.

Because the reinforcing gradient is present, the breeze shouldn't die at sunset the way a pure-thermal day would. The sea-breeze component itself collapses around 7:31 PM (roughly 30 minutes before the 8:01 PM sunset), but the onshore gradient keeps blowing after that, so expect a gradual easing and backing toward SW through 9–10 PM rather than a hard drop to nothing.

Pressure across the cove should be fairly even in SW-WSW flow, with a slight edge toward the east shore/mouth near Tod's Point per the cove geography — favor that side marginally rather than committing hard to either shore.

One flag: HRRR's raw hourly wind speeds (5–7 kt) are running noticeably lighter than what's actually on the water right now — Riverside YC is reading 10.7 kt sustained, gusting 17.4 kt, and buoy 44040 is at 12.7 kt gusting 18.3 kt. Model magnitude is a known soft spot for a maturing sea breeze; treat the speed numbers above as a floor, not a ceiling, especially in the first couple of hours.
